titleFa: کتاب More Speak English Like an American
titleEn: More Speak English Like an American
author: Amy Gillett
introFa: کتاب «More Speak English Like an American» نوشته Amy Gillett یکی از منابع ارزشمند و معتبر برای یادگیری زبان انگلیسی در سطح B2 است. این اثر با ساختاری منسجم و غنی، شما را در تسلط بر واژگان و درک مطلب یاری می‌کند.
readingTipsFa: پیش از مطالعه هر بخش از کتاب «More Speak English Like an American»، نگاهی سریع به تیترها و ساختار آن بیندازید.
واژگان و اصطلاحات جدید را در زمینه و بافت جمله یادداشت کنید تا در حافظه بلندمدت تثبیت شوند.
پس از پایان هر فصل، نکات کلیدی و آموخته‌های خود را مرور کرده و به زبان خود خلاصه کنید.

Are men really more full of SNOT? 13 January 2009 Sir, We read with interest a recent paper in which a small German study found that women with chronic rhinosinus- itis report poorer disease-speciﬁc quality of life than men.1 Using data from the National Comparative Audit of Sur- gery for Nasal Polyposis and Chronic Rhinosinusitis, we evaluated gender differences in symptom scores in a UK population using the Sinonasal Outcome Test (SNOT22). The full methodology and results of the audit have been reported previously in this journal.2 Data were collected prospectively on 3128 patients undergoing sinonasal surgery in 80 NHS Trusts in England and Wales, under the care of 298 consultant ENT surgeons. This included patients undergoing a wide range of surgi- cal procedures for chronic rhinosinusitis with or without nasal polyposis. Patients completed a preoperative questionnaire about their health status ⁄ symptoms, and previous treatments received. The main outcome measure was the SNOT-22, a validated modiﬁcation of the SNOT-20.2 Clinical data proforma were completed by surgeons for each operation, including results of preoper- ative imaging, clinical ﬁndings and extent of surgery per- formed. For this study, gender differences in preoperative SNOT22 scores, Lund-Mackay scores (a radiological score of disease severity) and polyp extent was evaluated. There is a clear gender difference in patient reported symptoms (Table 1), with women reporting signiﬁcantly higher preoperative SNOT22 scores than men. However, comparing preoperative markers of disease severity dem- onstrates that males in the cohort have more extensive disease than females. The change in SNOT22 score following sinonasal surgery is similar for both men and women, with men therefore achieving signiﬁcantly lower scores postoperatively (Fig. 1). conﬁrms that the gender difference persisted when other case-mix variables were simultaneously controlled for within a regression model. This ﬁnding was also conﬁrmed in a study of 116 patients assessed to determine the SNOT22 in a normal population. Women report higher levels of symptoms despite less extensive disease (determined by clinical markers of sever- ity), and this is likely to be due to a systematic difference in response style. Similar gender differences have been found using a global quality of life instrument, the SF-36,3 in a healthy population, where women indicate poorer health scores across all eight domains than men, despite longer life expectancy and lower rates of chronic illness. Findings are replicated across many disease groups, such as patients with cardiac disease4 and serious mental illness.5 These gender differences highlight the poor correlation between patient-reported symptom severity and objective measures of disease severity, which has been reported across many medical specialties. The relationship between physiological or radiological variables and symptoms is complex. It is likely that patients’ quality of life is the result of an interaction between many factors, in which biological variables are only a piece of the ﬁnal jigsaw. Symptoms will be modiﬁed by characteristics of the indi- vidual and environment in which he or she lives. These results suggest that gender is an important factor that modiﬁes patient-reported symptom severity. Women may perceive greater symptom burden, or alternatively may feel more able to report the full extent of their symptoms, particularly those more ‘emotional’ domains. Men really are more full of SNOT than women. However, contrary to popular belief, men seem to put up with more SNOT and report lower symptom sever- ity than their female counterparts despite more extensive disease.
